label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms**, and Trump agreed it played a part while defending the war (Fox News, Washington Examiner, CNBC). Democrats hold 54 Senate seats in NBC's count, but Mississippi is separated by a few dozen votes and has no recount process (NBC, The Hill, NPR). Rep. Massie plans a Hegseth impeachment vote when the House returns Nov. 9, and GOP sources told CNN they expect it to pass (CNN, The Hill). In California, Prop 40 trails with about 55% voting no while Prop 42 leads (CalMatters, KQED, Fox Business), and the regional transit tax passed (KQED, SF Chronicle). BART also picked developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station (SF Chronicle). The Dow gained 3.03% on Wednesday for its **best day since April 2025**, as Big Tech surged and AI data center names fell on Texas's moratorium push (CNBC, Bloomberg). The **October jobs report lands Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern**, with forecasts from 55,000 to 65,000 jobs and a December Fed hike in view (CNBC, Bloomberg). Qualcomm slid more than 9% premarket after handset chip sales fell 26% on memory costs (CNBC). NASA's Swift observatory re-entered over Sumatra, closing a 22-year **gamma-ray burst mission** (NASA, Space.com). Anthropic's IPO roadshow could start the week of Nov. 9, with no price range filed yet (CNBC, Bloomberg).

stories.title: Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms, and Trump partly agrees
stories.summary: Vice President Vance blamed the Iran war for the GOP rout, while Trump said Iran was part of it but defended the war.
story: Vice President JD Vance said this week that the Iran war cost Republicans the midterm elections, Fox News and the Washington Examiner reported. Vance argued the party must end the war, address the cost of living and change its approach to Israel. President Trump told reporters Iran played a role. "I think a part of it was Iran," he said, while insisting "Iran can't have a nuclear weapon" (Fox News). Democrats won both chambers of Congress on Tuesday (CNBC, NBC).

Axios reported, as cited by Fox News, that Vance privately urged Trump to seek a deal with Iran and warned the war was unpopular. Markets noticed. CNBC said oil fell more than 8% on Wednesday as Vance's post landed, and stocks extended their gains. Iranian officials, meanwhile, framed the results as a rejection of Trump's war (Fox News).

Republicans disagree about the cause. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer wrote that "the problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire," blaming mixed messaging (Fox News). Conservative commentators including Sean Davis of The Federalist and Matt Walsh of The Daily Wire called the result a wipeout and pointed to the war and high gas prices (Fox News). A Washington Examiner column cited exit polls in which 74% of voters called the Iran war a crucial or major factor.
The split matters for 2028. Fox News framed Vance's comments as the opening of a possible 2028 showdown over where the Republican coalition goes next.
facts: Vance blamed the Iran war for the GOP midterm losses (Fox News, Washington Examiner).
Trump said "a part of it was Iran" but called the war the right decision (Fox News).
Democrats won control of both chambers on Nov. 3 (CNBC, NBC News).
Oil fell more than 8% Wednesday as Vance's post circulated (CNBC).
Fleischer blames the cease-fire and messaging, not the war itself (Fox News).
stories.flag: The report that Vance privately urged Trump to seek a deal comes from Axios as cited by Fox News; I did not open the Axios piece.
stories.left: The war was a choice, and voters judged it. Gas prices rose, troops were put at risk, and the administration kept shifting its explanation, which Vance himself said mattered. Democrats argue the result is a rebuke of unilateral military action and of a White House that sidelined Congress on war powers.
stories.right: The war's goal, stopping a nuclear Iran, was sound, and the problem was execution. Fleischer's point is that a cease-fire that looked like retreat and muddled messaging cost more votes than the war itself. Many conservatives also say affordability and candidate quality drove losses, and that Trump should finish the job rather than abandon it.
stories.next: Watch whether Trump changes Iran policy in the lame-duck session; the House returns Nov. 9.

stories.title: Democrats hold 54 Senate seats in NBC's count as Mississippi hangs on a few dozen votes
stories.summary: Democrats swept Congress, but the Mississippi Senate race is separated by dozens of votes and the state has no recount process.
story: Democrats won control of both chambers on Nov. 3, according to NBC News, NPR and CNBC. NBC's Senate page shows Democrats at 54 seats after flipping seven Republican-held seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. On the House side, NBC projects 258 Democratic seats while CNBC's desk projected at least 245, so the final figure is still moving. The Hill reported Chuck Schumer is set to become majority leader.

Mississippi is the open question. NBC and CNN reported Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes, with the margin shifting between 28 and 65 as counting continued. The Hill and NBC report that Mississippi has no automatic or candidate-requested recount. A court would have to order one.

Colom's campaign says about 15,000 affidavit ballots remain, and they can be cured and counted until a Nov. 10 deadline, NBC reported. Colom said, "We're prepared to litigate." The Hyde-Smith campaign and the NRSC have set up a recount fund, according to an FEC filing cited by NBC.

The final Senate margin matters less for control, which Democrats already hold, than for the size of the majority Schumer can use on nominations and a Defense reconciliation package in the lame-duck session.
facts: NBC News shows Democrats at 54 Senate seats after seven GOP flips.
NBC projects 258 House seats for Democrats; CNBC projected at least 245.
Mississippi has no automatic or candidate-requested recount (The Hill, NBC).
About 15,000 affidavit ballots remain, per Colom's campaign (NBC).
The affidavit cure deadline is Nov. 10.
stories.flag: House and Senate totals differ between outlets and are still changing; the 15,000 ballot figure comes from the Colom campaign.
stories.blindspot: Mississippi count coverage found came from center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning reporting on the count was found.
stories.left: Voters gave Democrats a mandate on affordability, health care and corruption, as DNC chair Ken Martin put it. Every uncounted legitimate ballot in Mississippi should be counted, and the lack of any recount procedure is a gap in election law that Republicans and Democrats should both want fixed.
stories.right: A majority assembled on Republican unpopularity is not a mandate, as a Hill opinion piece argued. In Mississippi, the Hyde-Smith campaign is right to prepare for a legal fight over close counts and provisional ballots, since the rules for curing ballots decide who sits in the Senate.
stories.next: Mississippi's affidavit ballot cure deadline is Nov. 10; a court fight is possible after that.

stories.title: Massie plans a Hegseth impeachment vote when the House returns, and GOP sources expect it to pass
stories.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie will force a vote next week as Republicans such as Sen. Thom Tillis say Hegseth faces a reckoning.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie plans to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the House returns from recess on Nov. 9, CNN reported. CNN cited multiple GOP sources who expect the resolution to pass. Speaker Mike Johnson called it "a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention" that "will immediately be tabled" (CNN).

Massie introduced the privileged resolution in September. His 34-page measure accuses Hegseth of abusing the powers of his office over the Iran war and other actions, CNN and Bloomberg Government reported then. House leaders sent members home early to avoid the vote, which Massie called a dodge and Johnson denied (The Hill, NBC News).

Pressure has grown since the midterms. Sen. Thom Tillis said Hegseth faces "a reckoning" in the lame-duck session (The Hill), and Fox News reported a White House official suggested Trump may hold him accountable. Trump said Wednesday, "I think he's doing a very good job." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon told CNN he is leaning against impeachment.
Massie argues departing Republicans may be freer to vote their conscience now that they do not face voters.
facts: The House returns Nov. 9 and Massie says he will force the vote (CNN).
GOP sources told CNN they expect it to pass; Johnson says it will be tabled.
Sen. Tillis says Hegseth faces a reckoning in the lame duck (The Hill).
Trump said Wednesday Hegseth is doing a very good job.
Rep. Bacon is leaning against impeachment (CNN).
stories.flag: 'Expected to pass' comes from anonymous GOP sources; no vote has happened.
stories.left: Hegseth's conduct of an unpopular war and his handling of the Pentagon merit oversight, and impeachment is the Constitution's tool when a cabinet officer abuses his office. The election results show that voters want accountability, and Republicans who agree privately should vote that way publicly.
stories.right: Impeachment is a stunt when it is aimed at a cabinet secretary for policy disagreements, as Johnson argues. If Republicans think Hegseth should go, the president can fire him. Using the House to settle an intra-party fight over the war sets a precedent that Democrats will use against future Republican secretaries.
stories.next: The House returns Nov. 9; a motion to table or a vote on Massie's resolution could come that week.

stories.title: Conservative writers blame Trump, the Iran war and affordability for the Republican rout
stories.summary: National Review, the Free Press and the Washington Examiner give competing explanations for the GOP's midterm losses.
story: Right-leaning outlets are publishing blunt post-mortems. The Free Press's Eli Lake wrote that Trump squandered his comeback and cited his request that voters "pretend I'm on the ballot." National Review ran several pieces, one arguing Trump lost the congressional GOP by treating members with contempt, another saying Republicans must lead with governance, not resentment.

The Washington Examiner offered three angles. One column argued the party's problem was an unfinished Iran war and poor salesmanship, citing exit polls in which 74% of voters called the war a crucial or major factor. Another said Republicans lacked a compelling affordability answer and need one by 2028. A third quoted Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his primary to Ken Paxton, criticizing the party's "unforced political errors."

National Review also cited tariffs, corruption concerns and worries about AI as weakening the working-class coalition. The Examiner pushed back on one popular theory, arguing candidate quality was not the main cause.

On the other side, NBC News framed the result as Democrats winning on affordability, with the harder test being whether they can deliver lower costs. The Hill's opinion section argued Democrats won on someone else's unpopularity.
facts: Eli Lake of the Free Press argues Trump blew his comeback.
National Review says Trump's treatment of congressional Republicans contributed to defeat.
A Washington Examiner column cites exit polls: 74% called the Iran war crucial or major.
Cornyn criticized 'unforced political errors' after losing his primary to Paxton.
NBC News says Democrats won on affordability and now must deliver.
stories.flag: Most pieces are opinion columns, and the 74% exit poll figure is from one Examiner column.
stories.left: The lesson is that tariffs, an unpopular war and broken promises on prices have consequences. Democrats should avoid overreading the win and focus on lowering costs, as Jeffries and Schumer say, rather than on investigations alone.
stories.right: A thoughtful conservative reading is that the party lost its message and its discipline. Republicans need a credible affordability agenda, a clear end state in Iran, and a Congress treated as a partner rather than an obstacle.
stories.next: Watch the lame-duck session and the first Republican leadership fights before the new Congress is seated Jan. 3.

stories.title: Prop 40 billionaire tax appears headed for defeat while Prop 42 leads
stories.summary: Early counts show about 55% voting no on the one-time 5% billionaire tax, and the union behind it says it may return in 2028.
story: California's Prop 40, a one-time 5% tax on residents worth more than $1 billion, was failing in early returns, CalMatters, KQED and the SF Chronicle reported. KQED's tally with about 61% counted showed 44.7% yes and 55.2% no. Fox News and Fox Business also reported the measure was on track to fail.

Prop 42, which would bar new state taxes on financial assets, private businesses and pensions and prohibit retroactive taxes, was leading, and Prop 41 was trailing, according to CalMatters and KQED. If Prop 41 or 42 outpolls Prop 40, the tax cannot take effect. Gov. Gavin Newsom endorsed Prop 42 before the vote. The California Democratic Party and the state labor federation backed Prop 40, while the California Teachers Association opposed it (KQED).

SEIU-UHW, which sponsored Prop 40, said it would try again in 2028 if the Legislature "fails to deliver a real solution" to health care funding (KQED). Counts are incomplete and may not be settled until next week, the SF Chronicle noted.
Conservative outlets have argued the tax would backfire. The Washington Examiner cited an NBER paper finding it would likely leave California with less revenue.
facts: Prop 40 was at 44.7% yes and 55.2% no with about 61% counted (KQED).
Prop 42 would ban new wealth taxes and retroactive taxes.
Newsom endorsed Prop 42 before the vote.
The sponsoring union says it may return in 2028 (KQED).
Final results may take until next week.
stories.flag: Results are partial and not yet officially called.
stories.left: Progressives argue the measure was a response to a health care funding gap created by federal Medicaid cuts and that extreme wealth concentration deserves a one-time levy. Its defeat reflects a heavily funded opposition campaign and an intra-party split, not a rejection of the problem, and the union's 2028 threat shows the issue is not dead.
stories.right: Conservatives argue a retroactive tax on a few hundred people would have driven capital and taxpayers out of California and left the state with less revenue, as a paper cited by the Washington Examiner suggests. Voters across lines, and a Democratic governor, rejected it, and Prop 42 adds a lasting guardrail against wealth taxes.
stories.next: Final counts and the Prop 42 outcome are expected over the next week or so; certification is in early December.

stories.title: Regional transit tax passes, and BART picks developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station
stories.summary: Bay Area voters approved the regional transit sales tax, and BART chose a team to negotiate housing at Fremont Station.
story: Bay Area voters approved Regional Measure RTM and an S.F. Muni tax, the SF Chronicle and KQED reported. KQED headlined it "Death Spiral Averted." The measure adds a half-cent sales tax in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and a one-cent tax in San Francisco, set to expire in 14 years, projected to raise about $1 billion a year. KQED's Alameda County tally showed 61.4% yes.

Nearly 65% of Alameda County's share is steered to BART operations, (SF Chronicle, KQED). Opponents argued agencies should cut costs first. Results are preliminary, and certification is due in early December.

In Fremont, the SF Chronicle reported on Oct. 29 that the BART board chose Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing to negotiate a first phase of housing at Fremont Station, about 643 homes on land now used for surface parking. BART's site says 176 would be affordable, with a plaza and a new bike and pedestrian route from Mowry Avenue. It is an exclusive negotiating agreement, not a final deal, and the developer hopes for approval in 2027.
KQED's early results show Desrie Campbell, Kathy Kimberlin and Ying Min Li ahead in Fremont council races, though the page's timestamps were inconsistent.
facts: RTM is a half-cent sales tax in four counties and one cent in San Francisco for 14 years.
KQED's Alameda tally showed 61.4% yes.
BART board chose Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing for 643 homes at Fremont Station.
The Fremont deal is an exclusive negotiating agreement, not final.
Fremont council results are early and unconfirmed.
stories.flag: Fremont council results are early counts from a page with inconsistent timestamps.
stories.blindspot: Covered by Bay Area outlets that lean left-of-center; no right-leaning coverage of the transit tax or the Fremont housing deal was found.
stories.left: Transit is climate policy, an equity issue and an economic one, and voters chose to fund it. Putting 643 homes, 176 affordable, on BART parking lots is the kind of transit-oriented housing the region needs.
stories.right: Opponents argued agencies should cut costs before raising sales taxes for 14 years, and that sales taxes fall on working families. The burden is on the agency to show the money is well spent.
stories.next: Alameda County certifies results in early December; the Fremont housing deal needs approval, which the developer hopes to get in 2027.

stories.title: IRGC says tankers burned in Hormuz as Trump defends the Iran war
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the strait, one after hitting an Iranian mine.
story: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, with at least one blaze triggered when a tanker struck an Iranian undersea mine, Fox News reported. The IRGC said the vessels were using unauthorized routes through the strait.

The incident comes as the war's politics shifted. Trump acknowledged the war hurt Republicans but said he remains convinced it was right to stop Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, Fox News reported. A Fox headline on Nov. 4 said Trump threatened to "finish the job" if Iran rejects a nuclear deal while the IRGC vowed "united" resistance.

Background from earlier coverage: the U.S. continues a blockade of Iranian ports, and Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers to regain leverage over the strait (CNN, Fox News). CNBC reported oil fell more than 8% on Wednesday on hopes that a Democratic Congress will push Trump toward a deal.
Iranian officials framed the U.S. election results as an anti-war rebuke (Fox News).
facts: The IRGC said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in Hormuz on Thursday.
At least one fire was caused by a tanker hitting an Iranian mine, per the IRGC (Fox News).
The U.S. continues to blockade Iranian ports (Fox News).
Oil fell more than 8% on Wednesday (CNBC).
Iranian officials called the U.S. election results an anti-war rebuke.
stories.flag: The Hormuz incident is the IRGC's account as reported by Fox News; I found no independent confirmation.
stories.blindspot: Same-day Hormuz reporting found came mainly from Fox News; no independent or left-leaning confirmation was found.
stories.left: The war has no clear exit, it is raising energy prices and risking more American lives, and the election shows voters want it ended through diplomacy. A Democratic Congress should use funding and war-powers oversight to force a deal.
stories.right: Iran's mines and tanker attacks show why it cannot be allowed to hold the strait or a nuclear program. Trump's point is that a deal must truly block a bomb, and conservatives warn that walking away now would reward the IRGC.
stories.next: Watch for any announcement on U.S.-Iran talks and oil prices; the House returns Nov. 9.

stories.title: October jobs report arrives Friday with forecasts near 59,000 and a December Fed hike in view
stories.summary: ADP showed 86,000 private jobs, above forecasts, while economists expect 55,000 to 65,000 in Friday's official report.
story: The October jobs report is due Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect a gain of 59,000, Bloomberg's forecasters about 65,000 with unemployment steady at 4.2%, and FactSet 55,000 (CNBC, Bloomberg). The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed near 4.9% Thursday as traders waited (CNBC).

ADP said private employers added 86,000 jobs in October versus an expected 69,000, and weekly jobless claims came in at 189,000, below forecasts (CNBC, Fox Business). Axios reported the labor market held up in September data from JOLTS.

The Fed began hiking in September. Bloomberg said a solid report could keep it on track for more increases. CNBC reported markets priced more than a 77% chance of a December quarter-point hike as of Oct. 29, and September PCE inflation ran 3.6% against the 2% target.
The September payroll gain was only 29,000, and yields rose anyway (CNBC).
facts: Forecasts range from 55,000 (FactSet) to 65,000 (Bloomberg); Dow Jones consensus is 59,000.
ADP showed 86,000 private jobs versus 69,000 expected.
Weekly jobless claims were 189,000.
September PCE inflation was 3.6% year over year (CNBC).
The Fed's December meeting is Dec. 9.
stories.flag: The 77% December hike probability dates to Oct. 29 and may have changed.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found was from center and right-leaning business outlets; no left-leaning outlet coverage was found.
stories.left: With payrolls this weak, raising rates risks pushing workers into unemployment to fight inflation driven partly by tariffs and the oil shock. Democrats are expected to press for the Fed and the administration to weigh jobs and affordability together.
stories.right: Inflation at 3.6% is well above target and the Fed is right to keep hiking if the data allow. Conservatives also point to tariffs, spending and the war's oil shock, which the administration controls, as the real drivers of prices.
stories.next: October jobs report Friday, Nov. 6 at 8:30 a.m. ET; the Fed meets Dec. 9.

stories.title: Big Tech surges after the midterms while AI data center stocks fall
stories.summary: The Dow gained 3.03% on Wednesday, with Apple, Microsoft and Amazon up while CoreWeave and other neocloud names dropped.
story: The Dow jumped 1,569 points, or 3.03%, to 53,356 on Wednesday, its best day since April 2025, with the S&P 500 up 1.58% and the Nasdaq up 1.44%, CNBC reported. Investors read the Democratic win as removing political uncertainty, and oil fell more than 8%.

Bloomberg reported Amazon rose as much as 8.3%, Microsoft 7%, Alphabet 5.9% and Meta 3.6%, as traders bet a Democratic Congress will slow AI spending that is eating free cash flow. Apple jumped more than 6%. CNBC tied that to hopes that memory price pressure may ease.

AI infrastructure names went the other way. CoreWeave fell about 8%, with Iren and Nebius down 6%, after Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race on a data center moratorium platform, CNBC reported. Bloomberg said data-center-linked junk bonds opened weaker.
On Thursday, CNBC reported futures were mixed and Tesla and SpaceX fell again after Elon Musk's record election spending, at least $474 million, backfired.
facts: Dow +3.03% to 53,356; best day since April 2025 (CNBC).
Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet rose on a bet that Democrats will slow AI spending (Bloomberg).
CoreWeave fell about 8% and Iren and Nebius 6% (CNBC).
Futures were mixed Thursday (CNBC).
stories.why: The market is treating AI spending as a cost for the big buyers and a revenue source for the builders, so a policy slowdown helps the former and hurts the latter. Investors who hold both should watch which way regulation and Texas policy go.
stories.next: The October jobs report is Friday; Nvidia reports Nov. 17 after the close.

stories.title: AI data centers drive memory prices up, squeezing Apple and Qualcomm
stories.summary: Qualcomm guided below forecasts as handset chip sales fell 26%, and Apple's CEO called memory pricing unprecedented.
story: Qualcomm reported results above estimates on Nov. 4 but guided lower, CNBC reported. It forecast revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion and earnings per share of $2.15 to $2.35, against analyst expectations of about $10.48 billion and $2.27. Handset chip sales fell 26% to $5.14 billion because rising memory costs force phone makers to raise prices and hurt demand. Shares fell 7% after hours and more than 9% premarket.

Apple faces the same squeeze. At its latest earnings call, CEO John Ternus said, "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," and expected higher memory costs in the December quarter, TechCrunch reported. CNBC said Apple guided margins lower.

The cause is AI demand. CNBC and TechCrunch both describe data center buyers absorbing memory supply, which pushes up the cost of DRAM that phones and laptops need. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said, "We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue," about its data center business.
Several analysts cut Qualcomm price targets to between $185 and $200, according to CNBC.
facts: Qualcomm handset chip sales fell 26% to $5.14 billion (CNBC).
Qualcomm guided revenue to $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion.
Shares fell more than 9% premarket Thursday.
Apple's CEO called memory pricing 'unprecedented' (TechCrunch).
CNBC says Apple guided margins lower.
stories.flag: A TechCrunch headline cited a 154% Apple inventory jump; other coverage showed a smaller rise, so I did not use that figure.
stories.why: Memory is becoming the binding constraint for consumer hardware. Engineers will redesign around less memory, and device makers face a choice between higher prices and thinner margins.
stories.next: Watch memory contract prices and Apple's December quarter guidance.

stories.title: Nature Electronics paper puts a superinductor inside a standard silicon chip
stories.summary: Quantum Motion researchers describe a nonlinear superinductor built in a deep-submicrometre integrated circuit.
story: Nature Electronics published a paper on Nov. 4 describing a nonlinear superinductor in a deep-submicrometre integrated circuit, from Quantum Motion and collaborators. A superinductor is a component with very high inductance and low loss, used in superconducting circuits.

A related arXiv paper from Quantum Motion authors, "A superinductor in a deep sub-micron integrated circuit," builds the device in a 22-nm FDSOI chip using the high kinetic inductance of titanium nitride films. It connects to a silicon quantum dot on the same chip and demonstrates a radio-frequency single-electron transistor, a common readout sensor for semiconductor quantum computers.

The authors argue this could let digital and analog electronics and compact superconducting readout sit together on one chip. Quantum Motion builds silicon spin-qubit chips on standard foundry processes and raised $160 million in a Series C in May, according to SiliconANGLE.
I did not read either full paper, so the measured device performance should be checked against the source.
facts: Nature Electronics published the paper on Nov. 4, 2026.
The related preprint uses a 22-nm FDSOI process.
It uses titanium nitride thin films for high kinetic inductance.
It demonstrates an rfSET readout next to a silicon quantum dot.
Quantum Motion raised $160 million in May 2026 (SiliconANGLE).
stories.flag: I only saw the Nature Electronics title; the technical details come from the related arXiv preprint and may differ from the published paper.
stories.why: Scaling quantum computers to millions of qubits needs readout and control built with ordinary chip factories. Putting superconducting parts on the same chip as the qubits is a step toward that.
stories.next: Watch for follow-up results combining the superinductor with working qubits.

stories.title: NASA's Swift observatory re-enters over northern Sumatra after a failed rescue
stories.summary: The U.S. Space Force confirmed re-entry at 7:39 a.m. Eastern Wednesday; Swift leaves behind 22 years of open data.
story: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered the atmosphere on Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 7:39 a.m. Eastern, or about 4:39 a.m. Pacific, over northern Sumatra, the U.S. Space Force confirmed, according to NASA and Space.com. Re-entry was near 3.4 degrees north and 98.6 degrees east.

Swift's orbit decayed because of intense solar activity. A private rescue mission by Katalyst Space failed to meet up with the spacecraft, and NASA ended the mission Oct. 23, Space.com and NASA reported. Most of the roughly 1.5-ton spacecraft was expected to burn up, with a few dense parts possibly surviving. Space.com reported NASA put the odds of anyone being hurt at 1 in 2,100.

NASA says Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, and its rapid response helped show that short bursts likely come from neutron star mergers. Its archive holds nearly 22 years of data, all openly available.
NPR covered the end as a fiery finish to a mission that captured some of the universe's brightest events.
facts: Re-entry was confirmed at 7:39 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 4 over northern Sumatra.
Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts.
NASA ended the mission Oct. 23 after the rescue attempt failed.
NASA put the odds of injury at 1 in 2,100 (Space.com).
The data archive stays public (NASA).
stories.why: Swift's quick-reaction design made it the model for chasing cosmic explosions. Its data will keep producing papers, and its loss leaves a gap in rapid gamma-ray follow-up.
stories.next: Researchers will keep mining the Swift archive; NASA may publish a debris assessment.

stories.title: Mars hydrogen chloride near Alba Mons looks more like dust-and-ice chemistry than volcanism
stories.summary: Conference abstracts say hydrogen chloride detections near Alba Mons are hard to tie to volcanoes and may come from surface-atmosphere chemistry.
story: Hydrogen chloride on Mars was first spotted by the ACS instrument in two detections north of Alba Mons during northern summer. A later dedicated search in Mars years 37 and 38, using NOMAD and a ground telescope, found it again in the same area, according to conference abstracts. These are abstracts, not peer-reviewed papers.

The gas was first floated as a possible sign of magmatic activity. Researchers now say the evidence is weak. Other volcanic gases such as sulfur dioxide have not been detected, and detections are spread widely rather than clustered on one volcano.

Kevin Olsen's team proposes a cycle in which dust-lifted sodium chloride reacts with water vapor from sublimating polar ice to release chlorine, which then forms hydrogen chloride. Alba Mons's major volcanic activity ended much earlier than at Olympus Mons or the Tharsis Montes, which also makes a present-day source less likely.
ScienceAlert's coverage of the gas's discovery gives the background.
facts: ACS first detected HCl north of Alba Mons in northern summer.
A later search with NOMAD and a ground telescope found it again.
No other volcanic gases such as SO2 have been detected.
Olsen's team proposes a dust, salt and polar-ice chemical cycle.
The evidence comes from conference abstracts.
stories.flag: Based on conference abstracts, not peer-reviewed papers; the prior claim that this revives the question of active volcanism is not supported by these abstracts.
stories.why: A volcanic source would imply a geologically active interior. A chemical-cycle source would instead tell us how dust and water move through Mars's atmosphere.
stories.next: Watch for peer-reviewed papers from the ACS and NOMAD teams.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow could start the week of Nov. 9, with no price range yet
stories.summary: The public S-1 left the price blank; valuation talk runs from $1.4 trillion to $2 trillion.
story: Anthropic filed its public S-1 on Oct. 26 with the price range blank, according to coverage of the filing, with a planned Nasdaq listing under the symbol ANT. The range is expected in an amended filing before the roadshow, and press reports say the roadshow could begin the week of Nov. 9, with trading possibly before Thanksgiving. Anthropic has not announced a date.

Valuation expectations vary by outlet. Bloomberg reported on Oct. 27 that investors expect $1.4 trillion to $1.75 trillion, and CNBC reported the company is reportedly seeking $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Its last private valuation was $965 billion in May (Bloomberg). CNBC also reported Anthropic is considering offering 15% to 20% of shares to retail investors through JPMorgan.

Investors are split. CNBC's coverage was headlined that the IPO could be "speculative fiction" or a "generational moment," and a CNBC piece on Oct. 26 said an underperforming IPO could kick off a tech reset. Axios listed bullish and bearish signals from the filing.
Anthropic is the maker of Claude, so this edition's reporting on it relies on outside outlets.
facts: The public S-1 was filed Oct. 26 with the price blank.
The planned Nasdaq symbol is ANT.
Bloomberg reports expected valuations of $1.4 trillion to $1.75 trillion; CNBC says $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
The last private valuation was $965 billion in May.
Roadshow timing is based on unconfirmed press reports.
stories.flag: The week-of-Nov.-9 roadshow date is unconfirmed press reporting; I could not find a fresh amended filing.
stories.why: A listing at this scale would put a pure AI lab into public index funds and test whether revenue can outrun compute costs. How it trades could reset valuations across AI.
stories.next: Look for an amended S-1 with a price range, then a roadshow, possibly the week of Nov. 9.

stories.title: A Texas governor-elect who wants a data center moratorium puts the AI build-out on notice
stories.summary: Gina Hinojosa won on a statewide moratorium pledge, though Republicans still control the Legislature.
story: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race after campaigning for a statewide moratorium on new data center permits, CNBC reported. Projects already under construction would reportedly be exempt. She also wants to end industry tax breaks and require developers to cover their full electricity costs.

Texas holds about 25% of planned U.S. data center build, CNBC and TechCrunch reported. Neocloud stocks fell: CoreWeave dropped 8%, and Iren and Nebius 6%, while Bloomberg said data-center-linked junk bonds opened weaker. Big Tech stocks rose, adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point.

The limits on her power matter. Republicans still control the Legislature, which constrains what she can do. Nomura said much of the capacity due in 2027 is already under construction, while projects planned for 2028 face more exposure to permitting delays.

TechCrunch said a bigger clash over data centers could be coming after the midterms, and CNBC reported Democrats are seen as more favorable to moratoriums, with Elon Musk's spending in Texas backfiring.
facts: Hinojosa won on a statewide data center moratorium platform (CNBC).
Texas holds about 25% of planned data center build.
CoreWeave fell 8%; Iren and Nebius fell 6% (CNBC).
Republicans still control the Texas Legislature.
Nomura sees 2028 projects as most exposed.
stories.flag: CNBC articles give CoreWeave's fall as 8% in one and nearly 10% in another, so figures differ by time of day.
stories.why: Power, permitting and local politics are becoming the limit on AI capacity. A moratorium fight in Texas could move chip, power and credit markets.
stories.next: Watch the Texas Legislature's January session and Hinojosa's first budget and permit proposals.

briefs: Anthropic published a technical spec and code for FlashProve, an open-source system to cryptographically verify which AI model produced an output; researchers call it intermediate work with no deployment planned (TechCrunch).
A Science investigation reports neurotech headband makers have collected tens of millions of hours of brain-wave data and face few limits on using it to train AI (Science).
An anthrax outbreak has killed at least 30 hippos in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the past month, with no human cases reported so far (Nature).
Nature reports a simulation suggesting even a short delay before fleeing a tsunami can decide whether people reach safety (Nature, Nov. 4).
